title: Four Hours at the Dock, Six at the Closure: Canada's Winter Hours of Service Clock and Who Pays for It in 2026
summary: How Canada's 13/14/16 hours of service limits, cycles, deferral and adverse driving rules interact with dock detention and winter closures, and who pays.
body_markdown:
A driver comes on duty at 05:00 at a terminal in Mississauga for a live load in Brampton booked for 06:00. The trailer is loaded and the bills are signed at 10:30. He is eastbound on the 401 to a Montreal DC slot at 17:00 when squalls close the highway near Belleville. He sits in the queue, awake in the cab. By the time it reopens, his 14 hours on duty are gone, and so is the slot. Now three parties will argue over detention, a missed appointment fee and a driver who cannot take tomorrow's reload.


The scenario is illustrative. The closure is not far-fetched. On Jan. 27, 2026, squalls closed Highway 401 in both directions between Belleville and Trenton for much of the day after collisions involving about 50 vehicles. In B.C., heavy snow and multiple incidents closed the Coquihalla between Hope and Merritt from about 9:30 p.m. on Dec. 22, 2025 until around noon the next day.


The hours of service clock is the scarcest asset on a Canadian winter lane, and most of it is spent standing still. Every decision worth making this season is about who gets to spend it.


## The clock, as written


For extra-provincial carriers, the Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations (SOR/2005-313, current to Oct. 19, 2026 and last amended June 12, 2021) set the limits south of 60°N. A driver may not drive after 13 hours of driving or 14 hours of on-duty time in a day, and may not drive after 16 hours have elapsed since the end of the last period of at least 8 consecutive hours off duty. The day requires at least 10 hours off duty, including 2 hours outside the 8-hour block.


The definition of on-duty time is where winter and detention meet. It includes waiting before and while a commercial vehicle is loaded, unloaded or dispatched, and waiting at an en route point because of an accident or other unplanned occurrence. A closure queue is on-duty time unless the driver is genuinely resting in a qualifying sleeper berth.


## The tools that help, and the ones that do not


**Adverse driving conditions.** Section 76 lets a driver who meets snow, sleet, fog or other adverse conditions extend the 13 hours of driving and trim the 2 hours of extra daily off-duty time. Driving, on-duty and elapsed time cannot be extended by more than 2 hours, the driver must still take 8 consecutive hours off, and the trip must have been possible under normal conditions without the extension. The definition only covers conditions that were not known, and could not reasonably have been known, immediately before the driver began driving. A squall warning posted before departure is a known condition. Four hours at a shipper is not weather at all.


**Deferral.** Section 16 lets a driver push up to 2 hours of daily off-duty time to the next day if total off-duty time across the two days is at least 20 hours, total driving is no more than 26 hours, the deferred time is added to the 8-hour block on day two, and the record of duty status declares which day the driver is on. It cannot be combined with split sleeper berth time, and it operates "despite" the daily limits in sections 12 and 14 only. Section 13, and with it the 16-hour window, still governs.


**The sleeper berth.** A single driver in a qualifying sleeper berth can split off-duty time into two periods, neither under 2 hours, totalling at least 10, and a qualifying period is excluded from the 16-hour calculation. That makes a stopped closure queue a dispatch decision: log it as on-duty and burn the window, or, where it is safe, rest in the berth for a qualifying period and preserve it.


**Personal conveyance is not a rescue.** Off-duty personal use requires an unloaded vehicle, unhitched trailers and no more than 75 km in a day. A loaded driver out of hours 40 km from the receiver cannot drive the load in on personal use.


## Cycles decide what a weather layover buys


Cycle 1 caps on-duty time at 70 hours in 7 days. Cycle 2 caps it at 120 hours in 14 days, with no driving after 70 hours without 24 consecutive hours off. A reset takes 36 consecutive hours off in cycle 1 and 72 in cycle 2. Switching from cycle 1 to cycle 2 takes 36 hours off. Switching back takes 72.


For a cycle 1 driver, 36 hours stuck in Hope or Thunder Bay can become a full reset and a fresh week. For a cycle 2 driver, the same layover resets nothing. Planners who track cycles turn a lost weekend into recovered capacity.


## North of 60 and inside one province


Freight to Whitehorse and Yellowknife runs under different federal numbers. North of 60°N, a driver must take 8 consecutive hours off after more than 15 hours of driving or 18 hours on duty, and cannot drive once more than 20 hours have elapsed since the last 8-hour break. Cycle 1 allows 80 hours in 7 days. Lanes that cross the 60th parallel need both rule sets in the plan.


Carriers that never leave one province follow provincial rules. Ontario's O. Reg. 555/06 mirrors the 13, 14 and 16 hour limits and the cycles, but two details differ. Its adverse conditions provision adds up to 2 hours of driving and on-duty time only if the 16-hour elapsed limit is not exceeded, while the federal rule allows elapsed time to stretch by up to 2 hours. Its deferral rule also caps total on-duty time across the two days at 28 hours. Ontario has required certified ELDs for intra-provincial truck drivers since June 12, 2022.


Alberta's Drivers' Hours of Service Regulation (AR 317/2002) works on a work shift. A provincial driver may not exceed 13 hours of driving or drive after 15 consecutive hours on duty, needs 8 consecutive hours off before starting a shift, and may exceed driving limits by up to 2 hours in unexpected adverse conditions. Provincial guidance says one vehicle operating outside Alberta makes the carrier federally regulated.


## What the ELD records, and what it becomes


Federally, the driver must input or verify the cycle being followed and any section 16 deferral, and record the reason for any adverse conditions extension. Carriers must verify certified records against supporting documents and require corrections.


Supporting documents are where detention billing and compliance become the same file. They include dispatch and trip records showing arrival and departure times, government-issued documents indicating vehicle location, and bills of lading, kept for at least 6 months. The gate time you bill detention from is the record an auditor will compare against the log. If they disagree, you have a billing problem and a compliance problem at once.


The penalty for getting it wrong is time. An inspector can place a driver out of service for 10 consecutive hours for breaching the 13 or 14 hour daily limits, 8 hours for the mandatory off-duty rules in section 13, and 72 hours for tampering with records.


## Where the money leaks


Waiting costs twice, in hours and in pay. Under the Canada Labour Code's Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations, standard hours for federally regulated highway drivers may not exceed 60 a week, or 50 in a week with a paid general holiday. Dock waiting counts as working hours, and cycle 1 allows 70 on-duty hours in 7 days, so an employee driver can reach overtime well before the HOS limit. Christmas Day 2026 falls on a Friday and Boxing Day on a Saturday, so expect a short receiving week with a 50-hour standard for many drivers.


Drivers notice who absorbs it. In a survey of 404 Canadian drivers conducted in 2025 and released in February 2026 by driver advocacy and community legal groups, 74% of federally regulated drivers and 68% of provincially regulated drivers said they were not paid for all hours worked, with waiting at shippers, receivers and borders among the examples.


B.C. adds a fixed cost to the clock. From Oct. 1 to April 30, commercial vehicles with a licensed gross vehicle weight of 11,794 kg or more must carry steel chains on most major highways and install them where a chain-up is active. Chain-up time is on-duty time and belongs in the lane plan.


## What carrier, broker and hybrid leaders decide


**Asset carriers** decide how much clock a customer is allowed to consume. Plan from the receiver's actual dwell, not the appointment time. Refuse tenders that leave less than a set buffer against the 14 and 16 hours after expected dwell and chain-up. Make closure-queue handling, including when to go to the berth, a dispatcher instruction. Treat a 36-hour weather layover as a cycle 1 reset opportunity.


**Brokers** decide what they promise on hours they do not control. Rate confirmations should state the detention trigger, the evidence accepted (gate in, door, bills signed, gate out), the billing deadline and who approves. A rep who waives a carrier's detention to protect a shipper has made a pricing decision without authority. Do not book a same-day reload behind a dock with a four-hour history.


**Hybrids** decide which rules win when the brokerage asks the fleet to rescue a load. Decide in writing whether fleet HOS buffers apply to rescue loads, and whose scorecard absorbs the hours.


**Shippers and receivers** are named in the rules too. Section 4 says no motor carrier, shipper, consignee or other person shall request, require or allow a driver to drive in breach of the regulations. Put dwell limits and reallocation rules in the contract before January.


## Encoding the decisions


No two operations draw these lines the same way. A reefer fleet feeding northern Ontario grocery and a brokerage running GTA to Montreal retail need different buffers, approvers and exceptions. Rules in a planner's head disappear at 19:30 on a closed highway.


Serious shops encode them. Load statuses that separate waiting to load, loading, weather hold and closure queue, each with a timestamp and a person. Planning checks that compare remaining 13, 14, 16 and cycle hours, under the right federal or provincial rule set, against real dwell before tender. Permissions that limit who can waive detention or approve layover, and by how much. Billing rules that create detention charges from the same gate and door times kept as supporting documents. Customer visibility that shows the closure and the dock time, not just "late." The workflow should enforce decisions the business already made.


## FAQ


### Does time stuck at a highway closure count as on-duty time in Canada?


Yes, waiting at an en route point because of an accident or other unplanned occurrence is on-duty time under the federal regulations. Time genuinely spent resting in a qualifying sleeper berth is off-duty time.


### Can a driver use the adverse driving conditions extension for a forecast storm?


No, the extension only applies to snow, sleet, fog or other conditions that were not known and could not reasonably have been known immediately before the driver began driving. Where it applies, the extension is capped at 2 hours and the reason must be logged.


### Does deferring off-duty time extend the 16-hour window?


No, section 16 deferral operates despite the daily limits in sections 12 and 14 but does not override the 16-hour elapsed limit in section 13.


### How long does a driver need off to reset a cycle under federal rules?


A cycle 1 driver needs at least 36 consecutive hours off and a cycle 2 driver needs at least 72.


### Are Ontario and Alberta hours of service rules the same as the federal rules?


Not entirely. Ontario mirrors the 13, 14 and 16 hour limits but keeps the 16-hour limit firm under its adverse conditions rule, while Alberta uses a work shift model with 13 hours of driving and no driving after 15 consecutive hours on duty.
